title: North Berwick Witch Trials: James VI Personally Attends Interrogations
description: The North Berwick witch trials of 1590–1591 were the most sensational Scottish witch prosecutions of the sixteenth century, involving alleged conspiracy by a coven to murder King James VI through magic storms raised against his ship during his return from Denmark with his new queen. James personally attended interrogations and was reportedly convinced of witchcraft's reality by what he heard. Key accused included Agnes Sampson, John Fian, Euphame MacCalzean, and Barbara Napier; Sampson and Fian were executed after torture produced confessions of sabbath meetings, demonic pacts, and attempted regicide by wax images and storms. The king's personal involvement directly produced his Daemonologie (1597).
historiographical_note: Lawrence Normand and Gareth Roberts's Witchcraft in Early Modern Scotland (2000) provides a comprehensive study of the North Berwick trials with full documentation. The political dimension — the regicide conspiracy charge — is significant: Julian Goodare and others have analyzed how the Scottish judicial system's use of conspiracy charges intensified Scottish witch-hunting beyond English levels. The trials' direct connection to James's authorship of Daemonologie makes them unusually well-documented in terms of elite intellectual response.
source_method: Newes from Scotland (1591) pamphlet; Scottish trial records; Normand and Roberts (2000); secondary scholarship
